title: Shelton Powers Past Tiafoe to Reach Historic US Open Final
summary:
Ben Shelton is going to his first Grand Slam final — and he did it the hard way.

The 23-year-old American came from a set down to beat Frances Tiafoe 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 in an epic all-American semifinal at the US Open. The match lasted three hours and 17 minutes, and the crowd on Arthur Ashe Stadium was roaring the whole time.

Both players were chasing their first Grand Slam final. Neither seemed nervous. They traded dazzling shots and kept the fans on their feet. But in the end, it was Shelton who broke through.

"Frances is like a big brother to me," Shelton said. "Every time we get to take to this court together and play each other is super special."

Shelton's win makes history. He's the first Black American man to reach the US Open singles final since Arthur Ashe in 1972. He's also the first Black male player to reach any Grand Slam singles final since Jo-Wilfried Tsonga in 2008.

On Sunday, Shelton will face top seed Alexander Zverev. Zverev beat Karen Khachanov in straight sets to reach his third straight Grand Slam final. He's trying to win his second major of the year.

But here's the challenge: Shelton has lost all five of his previous matches against Zverev. Still, with the home crowd behind him, Shelton believes he can end a 23-year wait for an American men's singles champion at the US Open. Andy Roddick was the last American man to win it, back in 2003.

Shelton also shared an emotional message. His grandmother passed away earlier this year. "She's the reason my dad was able to play tennis," he said. "Without her, there's no Ben Shelton standing here today. This one is for her."

He added: "I'm going to leave it all on the court. Let's do this for the USA."
why_it_matters: Sport is one of the most visible places where a country sees who gets to succeed, and a 23-year-old breaking a 23-year national drought while becoming the first Black American man in the US Open final since 1972 shows how barriers can hold for decades before someone finally breaks through. For teenagers, it is a reminder that a bad head-to-head record or a long wait for someone 'like you' does not decide the next result.

background_read: The US Open is one of tennis's four Grand Slams — alongside the Australian Open, the French Open and Wimbledon — the biggest and most prestigious events in the sport, and its main stadium is named after Arthur Ashe (the first Black American man to win a Grand Slam singles title, at the 1968 US Open).

Ashe's legacy gives Shelton's run extra weight: Ashe reached the US Open final in 1972, and in the decades since, very few Black American men climbed that far in a sport that is expensive and difficult to break into without money and coaching.

The longer drought the article mentions is a different one: no American man at all has won the US Open singles title since Andy Roddick (the big-serving American champion who took the title in 2003), a gap that becomes a talking point in New York every summer.

Shelton's opponent, Alexander Zverev (a German star who has been ranked as high as No. 2 in the world and is known for his huge serve and long baseline rallies), has beaten Shelton in all five of their previous meetings — so the head-to-head record and the home crowd pull in opposite directions.
Jo-Wilfried Tsonga (the French player of Congolese descent who reached the 2008 Australian Open final) was the last Black man to play any Grand Slam singles final before Shelton.

perspectives.description: Shelton's run is a genuine milestone: the first Black American man in the US Open final since Arthur Ashe in 1972 and the first Black man in any Grand Slam final since Tsonga in 2008. It comes on merit, after a three-hour-plus win over a close friend, and it lifts an entire country's hopes for a home champion.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — the hype and the gap
perspectives.description: Shelton is 0-5 against Zverev, so some argue the 'history' framing oversells a match he is not favoured to win. Others point out that celebrating one breakthrough can hide the deeper problem — American men's tennis has produced no US Open champion since 2003, which is a system failure, not just a series of near-misses.

Men's tennis has been dominated for years by a small group of European players, and home crowds rarely decide Grand Slam finals. American tennis also has a long history of anointing 'the next champion' every few years, only for the wait to continue — which makes it hard to judge whether this is a turning point or another false dawn.

Whatever happens on Sunday, Shelton is 23 and Zverev is already an established top seed, so this final could mark the start of a long rivalry rather than a one-off. A win would reset expectations for American men at home Slams and likely draw more young players into the sport.
